text: Sections 25C-25E (lay-off compensation provisions) do not apply to establishments covered by Chapter VB, to establishments employing fewer than 50 workmen on average per working day in the preceding month, or to seasonal/intermittent-work establishments. 'Industrial establishment' here means a factory, mine, or plantation.
plain_english_summary: Small establishments (fewer than 50 workmen) and seasonal businesses are exempt from the statutory lay-off compensation regime in this Chapter -- relevant for early-stage startups below that headcount.

title: Definition of continuous service
text: A workman is in 'continuous service' if uninterrupted (interruptions for sickness, authorised leave, accident, legal strike, or lock-out/cessation not the workman's fault do not break continuity). If not literally uninterrupted, a workman is deemed to be in continuous service for one year if he actually worked at least 240 days (190 for below-ground mine work) in the preceding 12 months, or for six months if he worked at least 120 days (95 for below-ground mine work) in the preceding 6 months. Days counted as 'worked' include lay-off days, paid earned leave, temporary disablement from a work accident, and up to 12 weeks of maternity leave.
plain_english_summary: This is the key eligibility test for many protections (lay-off compensation, retrenchment compensation, etc.): does the employee have 'continuous service'? For most startup employees this comes down to the 240-days-in-12-months rule.

title: Right of workmen laid-off for compensation
text: A workman (other than a badli or casual workman) with at least one year of continuous service who is laid off must be paid, for each day of lay-off (excluding intervening weekly holidays), compensation equal to 50% of the total basic wages and dearness allowance he would otherwise have received; but if laid off for more than 45 days in any 12-month period, no compensation is payable for lay-off beyond the first 45 days if there is an agreement to that effect, and the employer may instead retrench the workman under section 25F after the first 45 days, adjusting past lay-off compensation against retrenchment compensation.
plain_english_summary: If a startup (above the size/threshold in section 25A) lays off eligible employees due to lack of work, it must pay 50% of wages for each lay-off day, with special rules kicking in after 45 days.

title: Duty of an employer to maintain muster rolls of workmen
text: Every employer must maintain a muster roll and allow workmen who present themselves for work at the appointed time to make entries in it, even during a lay-off.
plain_english_summary: A basic record-keeping duty proving who reported for work during a lay-off period, relevant to compensation claims.

title: Workmen not entitled to compensation in certain cases
text: No lay-off compensation is payable to a workman who refuses suitable alternative employment (not requiring special skill, offered at the same wages) at the same or another establishment of the same employer within 5 miles; who does not present himself for work at least once a day during normal hours; or whose lay-off is due to a strike or slow-down elsewhere in the establishment.
plain_english_summary: Carves out situations where a startup need not pay lay-off compensation, e.g. if it offers the employee equivalent alternative work nearby and the employee refuses it.

title: Conditions precedent to retrenchment of workmen
text: A workman with at least one year of continuous service cannot be retrenched until given one month's written notice (or pay in lieu) stating reasons, paid retrenchment compensation equal to 15 days' average pay per completed year of continuous service (or part thereof exceeding six months), and until notice is served on the appropriate Government in the prescribed manner.
plain_english_summary: This is the single most important compliance checklist for a startup laying off an eligible employee: 1-month notice (or pay in lieu), 15 days' pay per year of service as compensation, and a government notification.

title: Compensation to workmen in case of transfer of undertakings
text: Where ownership/management of an undertaking is transferred, a workman with at least one year of continuous service immediately before transfer is entitled to notice and compensation as if retrenched under section 25F, unless service is uninterrupted, terms are not less favourable, and the new employer is legally bound to honour continuity of service for future retrenchment compensation.
plain_english_summary: Relevant on an M&A/acquisition of a startup: employees are generally entitled to retrenchment-style compensation on a change of ownership, unless the buyer preserves continuity of service and terms.

title: Sixty days' notice to be given of intention to close down any undertaking
text: An employer intending to close down an undertaking must give the appropriate Government at least 60 days' prior written notice stating the reasons, except for undertakings employing fewer than 50 workmen on average, or construction-project undertakings; the Government may exempt an undertaking from this in exceptional circumstances (e.g. accident, death of employer).
plain_english_summary: Before winding down operations, a startup employing 50+ workmen must give the government 60 days' advance notice of the closure.

title: Compensation to workmen in case of closing down of undertakings
text: On closure of an undertaking for any reason, a workman with at least one year of continuous service is entitled to notice and compensation as if retrenched under section 25F; but if closure is due to unavoidable circumstances beyond the employer's control, compensation is capped at 3 months' average pay (mere financial difficulty, unsold stock accumulation, lease/licence expiry, or (for mining) mineral exhaustion do not count as 'unavoidable circumstances'). Special rules apply for construction undertakings closed on project completion.
plain_english_summary: If a startup shuts down entirely, employees are generally owed the same retrenchment-style compensation as a lay-off/retrenchment -- and note that simply running out of money or investor funding does NOT qualify as an 'unavoidable circumstance' that caps this compensation at 3 months.

title: Procedure for retrenchment
text: Absent an agreement to the contrary, an employer retrenching a workman must ordinarily follow 'last-in-first-out' within that category of workmen, unless the employer records reasons for a different order.
plain_english_summary: The default rule for choosing whom to retrench within a job category is 'last hired, first retrenched', unless the employer documents good reasons to deviate.

title: Re-employment of retrenched workmen
text: Where an employer proposes to hire again after retrenching workmen, retrenched Indian-citizen workmen who offer themselves for re-employment must be given an opportunity and have preference over other new applicants.
plain_english_summary: If a startup rehires after a round of layoffs, it must first offer the roles to the previously retrenched employees who want to return, ahead of hiring externally.

title: [Repealed]
text: This section (originally on recovery of moneys due from employers under this Chapter) was repealed by the Industrial Disputes (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1956, with effect from 10 March 1957. Recovery is now governed by section 33C.
plain_english_summary: Historical repealed provision; recovery of dues is now handled under section 33C.

title: Effect of laws inconsistent with this Chapter
text: This Chapter's provisions override any inconsistent law (including standing orders under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946), except that a workman keeps any more favourable benefit available under another law, rule, standing order, award or contract. This Chapter does not affect other State laws on settlement of industrial disputes, but lay-off/retrenchment rights/liabilities are governed by this Chapter.
plain_english_summary: A 'floor, not a ceiling' provision -- if a startup's contract or a State law offers better retrenchment/lay-off terms than this Chapter, the employee keeps the better terms.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS RELATING TO LAY-OFF, RETRENCHMENT AND CLOSURE IN CERTAIN ESTABLISHMENTS
title: Application of Chapter VB
text: This Chapter applies to a non-seasonal, non-intermittent industrial establishment (factory, mine or plantation) that employed not less than 100 workmen on average per working day in the preceding 12 months.
plain_english_summary: This much stricter regime (prior government permission needed for lay-off/retrenchment/closure) applies only once a startup crosses the 100-workmen threshold -- most early-stage startups will stay under Chapter VA instead.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS RELATING TO LAY-OFF, RETRENCHMENT AND CLOSURE IN CERTAIN ESTABLISHMENTS
title: Definitions
text: For this Chapter, 'industrial establishment' means a factory, mine, or plantation as defined in the respective Acts; and for companies with 51%+ Central Government paid-up share capital, or certain Parliament-established corporations, the Central Government is the appropriate Government.
plain_english_summary: Clarifies which establishments and which government (Centre vs State) this stricter Chapter applies to.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS RELATING TO LAY-OFF, RETRENCHMENT AND CLOSURE IN CERTAIN ESTABLISHMENTS
title: Prohibition of lay-off
text: In establishments covered by this Chapter, a workman (other than badli/casual) cannot be laid off without the prior permission of the appropriate Government/specified authority, unless the lay-off is due to shortage of power or natural calamity (and, for mines, also fire/flood/excess inflammable gas/explosion). The employer must apply in the prescribed manner, serving a copy on the workmen; the authority decides within 60 days (deemed granted if no order issues within 60 days); the order is binding for one year and reviewable/referable to a Tribunal. Lay-off without permission (or after refusal) is deemed illegal, entitling workmen to full benefits as if not laid off.
plain_english_summary: For 100+ workmen establishments, a startup cannot simply lay off employees -- it needs prior government permission except in narrow emergency circumstances (power shortage, natural calamity), and unauthorised lay-off is deemed illegal.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS RELATING TO LAY-OFF, RETRENCHMENT AND CLOSURE IN CERTAIN ESTABLISHMENTS
title: Conditions precedent to retrenchment of workmen
text: In establishments covered by this Chapter, a workman with at least one year of continuous service cannot be retrenched without 3 months' written notice (or pay in lieu) and prior permission of the appropriate Government/specified authority, obtained on application (served also on the workmen). The authority decides within 60 days (deemed granted if silent); the order binds for one year and is reviewable/referable to a Tribunal. Retrenchment without permission (or after refusal) is illegal. Where permission is granted/deemed granted, the workman is entitled to 15 days' average pay per completed year of continuous service.
plain_english_summary: For 100+ workmen establishments, retrenchment requires 3 months' notice (longer than the 1-month notice under section 25F) AND prior government permission -- a much heavier compliance burden than for smaller startups under Chapter VA.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS RELATING TO LAY-OFF, RETRENCHMENT AND CLOSURE IN CERTAIN ESTABLISHMENTS
title: Procedure for closing down an undertaking
text: An employer intending to close an undertaking covered by this Chapter must apply for prior permission at least 90 days before the intended closure date (except for construction-project undertakings), serving a copy on workmen's representatives. The Government decides within 60 days (deemed granted if silent); the order binds for one year and is reviewable/referable to a Tribunal. Closure without permission (or after refusal) is illegal, entitling workmen to full benefits as if not closed. On permitted closure, workmen get 15 days' average pay per completed year of continuous service.
plain_english_summary: A 100+ workmen startup cannot simply shut down -- it needs 90 days' advance notice and prior government permission to close, or the closure is deemed illegal and employees keep full entitlements as if the business never closed.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS RELATING TO LAY-OFF, RETRENCHMENT AND CLOSURE IN CERTAIN ESTABLISHMENTS
title: Special provision as to restarting of undertakings closed down before the 1976 Amendment
text: For undertakings closed before the Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 1976, if the Government is satisfied the closure was avoidable, restart is feasible, restarting would help worker rehabilitation or essential community supplies, and restart would not cause hardship to the employer, it may, after hearing both sides, direct restart within a specified time (at least one month).
plain_english_summary: A historical/transitional provision empowering the government to order the reopening of certain pre-1976 closed undertakings; unlikely to be relevant to a new startup.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS RELATING TO LAY-OFF, RETRENCHMENT AND CLOSURE IN CERTAIN ESTABLISHMENTS
title: Penalty for lay-off and retrenchment without previous permission
text: An employer contravening section 25M or 25N is punishable with imprisonment up to one month, or fine up to Rs. 1,000, or both.
plain_english_summary: Criminal penalty for a 100+ workmen employer that lays off or retrenches without the required prior government permission.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS RELATING TO LAY-OFF, RETRENCHMENT AND CLOSURE IN CERTAIN ESTABLISHMENTS
title: Penalty for closure
text: An employer closing an undertaking without complying with section 25-O(1) is punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine up to Rs. 5,000, or both. Contravening a refusal order or a section 25P restart direction attracts imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to Rs. 5,000, or both, plus a further fine up to Rs. 2,000 per day of continuing contravention after conviction.
plain_english_summary: Criminal penalty for closing a 100+ workmen establishment without following the mandatory permission procedure.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS RELATING TO LAY-OFF, RETRENCHMENT AND CLOSURE IN CERTAIN ESTABLISHMENTS
title: Certain provisions of Chapter VA to apply
text: Sections 25B (continuous service), 25D (muster rolls), 25FF (transfer compensation), 25G (retrenchment procedure), 25H (re-employment preference) and 25J (overriding effect) of Chapter VA also apply to establishments covered by this Chapter.
plain_english_summary: Extends several Chapter VA protections (continuous service definition, muster rolls, transfer compensation, LIFO procedure, recall rights) to the larger 100+ workmen establishments covered by Chapter VB as well.

title: Prohibition of unfair labour practice
text: No employer, workman, or trade union (registered or not) shall commit any unfair labour practice, as specified in the Fifth Schedule.
plain_english_summary: A blanket ban on the wide range of unfair practices listed in the Fifth Schedule -- e.g., victimising union activists, sham layoffs, coercive tactics -- applicable to both employers and unions/workmen.

title: Penalty for committing unfair labour practices
text: Any person committing an unfair labour practice is punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine up to Rs. 1,000, or both.
plain_english_summary: Criminal penalty attaching to any unfair labour practice under section 25T.

title: Penalty for illegal strikes and lock-outs
text: A workman who commences, continues, or furthers an illegal strike is punishable with imprisonment up to one month, or fine up to Rs. 50, or both. An employer who commences, continues or furthers an illegal lock-out is punishable with imprisonment up to one month, or fine up to Rs. 1,000, or both.
plain_english_summary: Criminal penalties for participating in (workman) or declaring (employer) an illegal strike/lock-out -- note the employer's fine cap is much higher than the workman's.

title: Penalty for instigation, etc.
text: Any person who instigates or incites others to take part in, or otherwise acts in furtherance of, an illegal strike or lock-out is punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine up to Rs. 1,000, or both.
plain_english_summary: Even without directly participating, inciting an illegal strike/lock-out attracts a penalty.

title: Penalty for giving financial aid to illegal strikes and lock-outs
text: Anyone who knowingly spends or applies money in direct furtherance of an illegal strike or lock-out is punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine up to Rs. 1,000, or both.
plain_english_summary: Criminalises funding an illegal strike/lock-out, matching the prohibition in section 25.

title: Penalty for breach of settlement or award
text: Anyone who breaches a binding settlement or award term is punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine, or both (with a further fine up to Rs. 200/day for a continuing breach after conviction); the court may direct compensation to the person injured by the breach be paid out of the fine.
plain_english_summary: If a startup (or its employees) breaches an agreed settlement or a Tribunal award, that breach is itself a criminal offence, with an ongoing daily fine for continued non-compliance.

title: Penalty for disclosing confidential information
text: Wilfully disclosing information required to be kept confidential under section 21, on complaint by the affected union or business, is punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine up to Rs. 1,000, or both.
plain_english_summary: Backs up the confidentiality obligation in section 21 with a criminal penalty for wilful disclosure.

title: Penalty for closure without notice
text: An employer closing an undertaking without complying with section 25FFA (60 days' notice) is punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine up to Rs. 5,000, or both.
plain_english_summary: Criminal penalty specifically for skipping the 60-day closure notice required under section 25FFA (for establishments below the Chapter VB threshold).

title: Penalty for other offences
text: An employer contravening section 33 (status quo during pending proceedings) is punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine up to Rs. 1,000, or both. Any other contravention of the Act or rules for which no other penalty is specified is punishable with a fine up to Rs. 100.
plain_english_summary: A catch-all penalty provision, plus a specific penalty for violating the 'no unilateral change during pending proceedings' rule in section 33.

title: Offences by companies, etc.
text: Where a company, other body corporate, or association of persons commits an offence under this Act, every director, manager, secretary, agent or other officer/person concerned with its management is deemed guilty of the offence, unless he proves it was committed without his knowledge or consent.
plain_english_summary: Directors/officers/managers of a startup can be personally held criminally liable for the company's offences under this Act, unless they can prove lack of knowledge or consent.

title: Conditions of service, etc., to remain unchanged during pendency of proceedings
text: During pending conciliation/arbitration/adjudication of a dispute, an employer cannot, without the authority's written permission, alter (to the workman's prejudice) conditions of service connected with the dispute, or discharge/punish a workman for dispute-connected misconduct. For matters not connected with the dispute, changes/discipline can be made per standing orders/contract, but discharge/dismissal requires paying one month's wages and applying for the authority's approval. Special added protection applies to 'protected workmen' (recognised trade union office-bearers, capped at 1% of workforce, min. 5 / max. 100), who cannot be disciplined/dismissed even for unconnected matters without the authority's prior written permission.
plain_english_summary: During an active dispute, a startup is significantly restricted from changing terms or disciplining/dismissing the workman(s) involved in that dispute without prior approval from the conciliation/adjudication authority -- and 'protected workmen' (recognised union representatives) get an even stronger shield.

title: Special provision for adjudication where section 33 is contravened
text: Where an employer contravenes section 33 during pending proceedings, the aggrieved employee may complain in the prescribed manner to the conciliation officer/Board (who factors it into settlement efforts), or to the arbitrator/Labour Court/Tribunal/National Tribunal (which adjudicates the complaint as if it were a referred dispute and submits its award to the Government).
plain_english_summary: Gives employees a direct complaint route if a startup violates the 'no unilateral change' rule in section 33 while a dispute is pending.

title: Power to transfer certain proceedings
text: The appropriate Government may, by written order with reasons, withdraw a pending proceeding from one Labour Court/Tribunal/National Tribunal and transfer it to another (including transferring a pending section 33/33A matter from a Tribunal/National Tribunal to a Labour Court); the receiving forum may continue from the transfer stage or start afresh, subject to any special directions.
plain_english_summary: An administrative provision allowing the government to reassign a pending case to a different court/tribunal.

title: Recovery of money due from an employer
text: A workman (or authorised representative, or heir if deceased) to whom money is due from an employer under a settlement, award, or Chapter VA/VB, may apply to the appropriate Government for recovery (within one year, extendable for sufficient cause); the Government, if satisfied, issues a recovery certificate to the Collector, recoverable as an arrear of land revenue. Disputed amounts/benefit valuations may be decided by a specified Labour Court (which may appoint a commissioner to value benefits), generally within 3 months, with the decision forwarded to the Government for recovery. Multiple workmen owed money by the same employer can file a joint application.
plain_english_summary: This is the practical enforcement mechanism for unpaid dues under an award/settlement/Chapter VA-VB entitlement: the employee applies to the government, which can recover the amount from the employer like a tax arrear -- a powerful, fast-track recovery route.

title: Cognizance of offences
text: No court shall take cognizance of an offence under this Act (or its abetment) except on a complaint made by or under the authority of the appropriate Government. No court inferior to a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class may try such an offence.
plain_english_summary: Criminal prosecutions under this Act can only be initiated with government authorisation, and must be tried by a sufficiently senior magistrate.

title: Protection of persons
text: A person refusing to take part or continue in an illegal strike/lock-out cannot, by reason of that refusal, be expelled from a trade union/society, fined, penalised, or disadvantaged compared to other members; the Civil Court may order restoration to membership or compensation instead.
plain_english_summary: Protects individual workers who refuse to join an illegal strike from retaliation by their own union/society.

title: Representation of parties
text: A workman may be represented by an office-bearer of his registered trade union (or its federation), or, if not a union member, by another authorised workman/union connected to the industry. An employer may be represented by an officer of his employers' association (or federation), or another authorised employer/association in the industry. No party may be represented by a legal practitioner in conciliation proceedings or before a Court; before a Labour Court/Tribunal/National Tribunal, legal representation requires the other parties' consent and the forum's leave.
plain_english_summary: Lawyers are generally NOT allowed to represent a startup (or its employees) in conciliation, and even before a Labour Court/Tribunal, using a lawyer requires the other side's consent plus the tribunal's permission -- representation is otherwise meant to be via trade/employer associations.

title: Power to remove difficulties
text: If a difficulty or doubt arises as to interpreting a provision of an award or settlement, the appropriate Government may refer the question to a Labour Court/Tribunal/National Tribunal, whose decision (after hearing the parties) is final and binding.
plain_english_summary: Provides a formal route to resolve ambiguity in the wording of an existing award or settlement.

title: Power to exempt
text: Where the appropriate Government is satisfied that adequate dispute-resolution mechanisms already exist for workmen in a government-department-run establishment (or class of establishments), it may, by notification, exempt that establishment/class conditionally or unconditionally from all or any provisions of the Act.
plain_english_summary: Allows exemption of certain government-run establishments that already have their own equivalent dispute-resolution systems.

title: Protection of action taken under the Act
text: No suit, prosecution, or other legal proceeding lies against any person for anything done, or intended to be done, in good faith under this Act or its rules.
plain_english_summary: Shields good-faith actions taken under the Act (e.g., by conciliation officers, employers following the Act) from separate legal liability.

title: Power to make rules
text: The appropriate Government may, after previous publication, make rules to give effect to this Act, covering matters such as procedure and powers of the authorities, arbitration agreement form, Works Committee constitution, salaries/allowances of presiding officers, strike/lock-out notice format, and conditions for legal representation. Rules may impose a fine up to Rs. 50 for contravention, and Central Government rules must be laid before Parliament (State rules before the State Legislature).
plain_english_summary: The umbrella rule-making power under which detailed procedural rules (state-specific and central) are issued to operationalise this Act.

title: Delegation of powers
text: The appropriate Government may, by notification, delegate any of its powers under the Act or rules to a subordinate officer/authority (Central Government to a State Government or its officers where appropriate Government is Central; State Government to its own officers where State is appropriate Government).
plain_english_summary: Administrative delegation provision allowing day-to-day exercise of statutory powers by subordinate officials.

title: Power to amend Schedules
text: The appropriate Government may, by notification, add industries to the First Schedule (public utility services) where expedient/necessary in the public interest. The Central Government may add to, alter, or amend the Second or Third Schedule. Every such notification must be laid before the State Legislature or Parliament, as applicable.
plain_english_summary: The mechanism by which the government updates which industries count as 'public utility services' or expands the jurisdictional Schedules of Labour Courts/Tribunals -- a startup's classification as a 'public utility service' can change via this route.

title: Industries which may be declared to be Public Utility Services
text: Lists industries the Government may declare 'public utility services' under section 2(n)(vi): transport (other than railways) of passengers/goods by land or water; banking; cement; coal; cotton textiles; food stuffs; iron and steel; defence establishments; hospital/dispensary service; fire brigade service; India Government Mints; India Security Press; copper, lead, zinc and iron-ore mining; oilfield service; uranium industry service; pyrites mining; Security Paper Mill, Hoshangabad; Bank Note Press, Dewas; phosphorite mining; magnesite mining.
plain_english_summary: If a startup's sector is on this list (or is later notified as such under section 40), the much stricter public-utility strike/lock-out notice rules in section 22 apply.

title: Matters within the jurisdiction of Labour Courts
text: The propriety/legality of an employer's order under standing orders; application and interpretation of standing orders; discharge or dismissal of workmen including reinstatement/relief for wrongful dismissal; withdrawal of customary concession/privilege; legality of a strike or lock-out; and all matters other than those in the Third Schedule.
plain_english_summary: Individual dismissal/discharge disputes and standing-orders disputes -- the matters most likely to affect a startup's day-to-day HR issues -- fall under Labour Court jurisdiction.

title: Matters within the jurisdiction of Industrial Tribunals
text: Wages (period/mode of payment); compensatory and other allowances; hours of work and rest intervals; leave with wages and holidays; bonus, profit sharing, provident fund and gratuity; shift working otherwise than per standing orders; classification by grades; rules of discipline; rationalisation; retrenchment of workmen and closure of establishment; and any other prescribed matter.
plain_english_summary: Broader/structural HR matters -- wage structures, bonus/PF/gratuity disputes, retrenchment and closure -- go to Industrial Tribunals rather than Labour Courts.

title: Conditions of service for change of which notice is to be given
text: Wages (period/mode of payment); employer's PF/pension fund contributions; compensatory and other allowances; hours of work and rest intervals; leave with wages and holidays; starting/altering/discontinuing shift working otherwise than per standing orders; classification by grades; withdrawal of customary concession/privilege or usage change; introduction/alteration of discipline rules (except as in standing orders); rationalisation/standardisation/improvement of plant or technique likely to cause retrenchment; and increase/reduction (other than casual) in personnel not caused by circumstances beyond the employer's control.
plain_english_summary: This is the exact checklist of changes that trigger the 21-day advance notice requirement under section 9A -- essentially any material change to pay, hours, leave, shift patterns, discipline rules, or headcount.

title: Unfair Labour Practices
text: Part I lists unfair labour practices by employers/employers' unions: interfering with workmen's right to unionise (e.g., threatening dismissal or lock-out for unionising, favouring specific unions); dominating/financially supporting a union or setting up employer-sponsored unions; discriminatory action against union activity (discharge, seniority changes, denied promotions); mala fide/victimising discharge or dismissal (false implication, disregard of natural justice, disproportionate punishment for minor misconduct); using contractors to break a strike; mala fide transfers; forcing 'good conduct bonds' as a precondition to resuming work after a legal strike; favouritism; indefinitely keeping workers as badlis/casuals/temporaries to deny permanent status; retaliation for testifying in an industrial dispute inquiry; recruiting during a legal strike; failing to implement an award/settlement/agreement; violence; refusing to bargain in good faith; and continuing an illegal lock-out. Part II lists unfair labour practices by workmen/unions: supporting an illegal strike; coercive unionisation tactics (physical picketing blockades, intimidation); bad-faith refusal to bargain; coercive activity against certification of a bargaining representative; 'go-slow', squatting, or gherao actions; demonstrations at residences of employer/managerial staff; wilful damage to employer property; and violence/intimidation to keep workers from attending work.
plain_english_summary: A detailed two-sided checklist of prohibited conduct -- Part I is the compliance list startups must avoid (e.g., do not victimise union activists, do not keep staff perpetually as 'temporary' to dodge permanent-employee protections, do not use contractors to break a strike), and Part II lists prohibited union/employee tactics like gherao and go-slow.

title: Short title, extent and application
text: This Act may be called the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946. It extends to the whole of India.

sub_structure.3: (3) It applies to every industrial establishment employing 100 or more workmen, or that employed that many on any day in the preceding twelve months; the appropriate Government may, after two months' notice, extend it by notification to establishments with fewer than 100 workmen.
sub_structure.4: (4) The Act does not apply to industries covered by Chapter VII of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, or to industrial establishments covered by the Madhya Pradesh Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1961 — except that it always applies to establishments under the Central Government's control, regardless of the Madhya Pradesh Act.

plain_english_summary: Names the Act, extends it across India, and sets its basic coverage threshold at 100 or more workmen (extendable downward by notification), while excluding establishments already governed by certain State-specific industrial relations laws, subject to a carve-out preserving coverage of Central Government establishments.

title: Interpretation
text: In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, the following terms have the meanings set out below.

sub_structure.a: "appellate authority" means an authority notified by the appropriate Government to hear appeals under the Act in a specified area; an Industrial Court or other authority already hearing a pending appeal when the 1963 amendment commenced is deemed the appellate authority for that appeal.
sub_structure.b: "appropriate Government" means the Central Government for establishments under Central Government control, a Railway administration, or a major port/mine/oilfield, and the State Government otherwise; disputes over whether an establishment is under Central Government control are decided finally by the Central Government after hearing the parties.
sub_structure.c: "Certifying Officer" means a Labour Commissioner, Regional Labour Commissioner, or any other officer notified by the appropriate Government to perform Certifying Officer functions.
sub_structure.d: "employer" means the owner of a covered industrial establishment, including a named factory manager, the government-appointed authority (or department head) for a government-controlled establishment, or any person responsible to the owner for supervising and controlling any other industrial establishment.
sub_structure.e: "industrial establishment" means an establishment as defined under the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, a factory under the Factories Act, 1948, a railway under the Indian Railways Act, 1890, or the establishment of a contractor who employs workmen to fulfil a contract with an industrial establishment's owner.
sub_structure.g: "standing orders" means rules relating to the matters listed in the Schedule.
sub_structure.h_i: "trade union" means a union registered under the Indian Trade Unions Act, 1926; "wages" and "workman" take the meanings given in the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.

plain_english_summary: Defines the Act's key actors and concepts: who counts as an 'employer' and what qualifies as a covered 'industrial establishment', and clarifies that 'standing orders' means the formal workplace rules the Schedule requires employers to spell out.

title: Submission of draft standing orders
text: Within six months of the Act becoming applicable to an industrial establishment, the employer must submit five copies of draft standing orders to the Certifying Officer for adoption in that establishment.

sub_structure.2: (2) The draft must cover every applicable Schedule matter, and should follow any prescribed model standing orders as closely as practicable.
sub_structure.3: (3) The draft must be accompanied by a statement giving prescribed particulars of the establishment's workmen, including any trade union they belong to.
sub_structure.4: (4) Subject to prescribed conditions, a group of employers running similar establishments may submit a joint draft.

plain_english_summary: Requires employers to formally draft and submit proposed workplace rules covering all the Schedule topics within six months of coverage beginning, ideally following any government model, with details of the workforce attached.

title: Conditions for certification of standing orders
text: Standing orders are certifiable under the Act if they cover every applicable Schedule matter and otherwise conform to the Act's provisions.

sub_structure.adjudication: It is the Certifying Officer's or appellate authority's function to adjudicate on whether the standing orders' provisions are fair or reasonable.

plain_english_summary: Sets the certification test for standing orders: full Schedule coverage plus general conformity with the Act, with the Certifying Officer or appellate authority empowered to judge fairness and reasonableness, not just formal completeness.

title: Certification of standing orders
text: On receiving the draft, the Certifying Officer forwards a copy to the workmen's trade union (or the workmen directly if there is none), with notice inviting objections within fifteen days.

sub_structure.2: (2) After hearing the employer and the trade union or other prescribed workmen's representatives, the Certifying Officer decides what modifications or additions are needed to make the draft certifiable, by written order.
sub_structure.3: (3) The Certifying Officer then certifies the draft (with any required modifications) and, within seven days, sends authenticated copies of the certified standing orders and the order to the employer and the workmen's representatives.

plain_english_summary: Sets out the certification process itself: the workforce gets a chance to object, the Certifying Officer decides on any necessary changes after hearing both sides, and then formally certifies and circulates the final standing orders.

title: Appeals
text: An employer, workmen, trade union, or other prescribed workmen's representatives aggrieved by the Certifying Officer's order may appeal to the appellate authority within thirty days of the copies being sent; the appellate authority's decision, confirming the standing orders as certified or amending them as needed for certifiability, is final.

sub_structure.2: (2) Within seven days of its order, the appellate authority sends copies to the Certifying Officer, employer, and workmen's representatives, along with the amended standing orders if it changed them.

plain_english_summary: Provides a thirty-day appeal window against a Certifying Officer's decision, with the appellate authority having the final word on what the standing orders should say.

title: Date of operation of standing orders
text: Standing orders take effect thirty days after authenticated copies are sent under section 5(3), unless an appeal is filed, in which case they take effect seven days after the appellate authority's order copies are sent under section 6(2).
plain_english_summary: Fixes exactly when new or modified standing orders become legally operative, giving a short buffer period and an extended timeline if the certification is appealed.

title: Register of standing orders
text: The Certifying Officer must file a copy of all finally certified standing orders in a prescribed register, and must supply a copy to anyone who applies and pays the prescribed fee.
plain_english_summary: Creates a public record of certified standing orders that anyone can access on payment of a fee, ensuring transparency about workplace rules.

title: Posting of standing orders
text: The employer must prominently post the text of the finally certified standing orders, in English and in the language understood by most of the workmen, on special notice boards near the main entrance and in every department where workmen are employed.
plain_english_summary: Requires employers to actively display the certified standing orders where workers will actually see them, in a language they understand, rather than merely filing them away.

title: Duration and modification of standing orders
text: Certified standing orders cannot be modified, except by agreement between the employer and the workmen (or a trade union/other representative body), until six months have passed since they (or their last modification) took effect.

sub_structure.2: (2) After that period, an employer, workman, or trade union/representative body may apply to the Certifying Officer for modification, submitting five copies of the proposed changes and, if by agreement, a certified copy of that agreement.
sub_structure.3: (3) The Act's provisions on first certification apply equally to a modification application.
sub_structure.4: (4) Sub-section (2) does not apply to industrial establishments where the appropriate Government is the Government of Gujarat or Maharashtra.

plain_english_summary: Locks certified standing orders in place for at least six months to give them stability, after which either side can seek changes through the same certification process, with a special carve-out for Gujarat and Maharashtra.

title: Payment of subsistence allowance
text: Where an employer suspends a workman pending investigation or inquiry into misconduct charges, the employer must pay subsistence allowance at 50% of the workman's prior wages for the first ninety days of suspension, rising to 75% for the remaining period if the delay in completing disciplinary proceedings is not attributable to the workman's own conduct.

sub_structure.2: (2) A dispute over subsistence allowance may be referred by either party to the local Labour Court under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, whose decision, after hearing both sides, is final and binding.
sub_structure.3: (3) If a State's other applicable law provides more beneficial subsistence-allowance terms, that law applies instead.

plain_english_summary: Guarantees suspended workers a minimum income during misconduct investigations, with the payment rate rising if the employer takes too long to conclude the inquiry, backed by a dispute-resolution route through the Labour Court.

title: Certifying Officers and appellate authorities to have powers of civil court
text: Every Certifying Officer and appellate authority has all the powers of a Civil Court for receiving evidence, administering oaths, compelling witness attendance, and compelling document discovery/production, and is deemed a civil court for certain Code of Criminal Procedure purposes.

sub_structure.2: (2) Clerical or arithmetical mistakes, or errors from accidental slips or omissions, in any order of a Certifying Officer or appellate authority may be corrected at any time by that officer/authority or their successor.

plain_english_summary: Gives Certifying Officers and appellate authorities real evidentiary powers equivalent to a civil court, while allowing simple clerical errors in their orders to be fixed at any time without a fresh proceeding.

title: Oral evidence in contradiction of standing orders not admissible
text: No oral evidence that would add to, vary, or contradict finally certified standing orders may be admitted in any court.
plain_english_summary: Protects the integrity of certified standing orders by barring courts from letting oral testimony override or reinterpret their written terms.

title: Temporary application of model standing orders
text: From the date the Act becomes applicable to an establishment until its own certified standing orders come into operation under section 7, the prescribed model standing orders are deemed adopted in that establishment, with the posting requirement (section 9) and certain other provisions (sections 13(2) and 13A) applying to them as if they were the certified standing orders.

sub_structure.2: (2) This section does not apply to industrial establishments where the appropriate Government is the Government of Gujarat or Maharashtra.

plain_english_summary: Fills the gap between an establishment first becoming covered by the Act and its own standing orders being certified, by automatically applying the government's model standing orders in the interim (except in Gujarat and Maharashtra).

title: Penalties and procedure
text: An employer who fails to submit draft standing orders as required, or who modifies standing orders other than in accordance with section 10, is punishable with a fine up to five thousand rupees, plus up to two hundred rupees per day for a continuing offence.

sub_structure.2: (2) An employer who contravenes the finally certified standing orders is punishable with a fine up to one hundred rupees, plus up to twenty-five rupees per day for a continuing offence.
sub_structure.3: (3) No prosecution under this section may be instituted without the appropriate Government's prior sanction.
sub_structure.4: (4) No court below a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the second class may try an offence under this section.

plain_english_summary: Sets the Act's penalty structure — heavier fines for failing to submit or improperly modifying standing orders, lighter fines for simply breaching certified standing orders, both escalating for continuing violations — with prosecutions requiring government sanction and a minimum-rank court.

title: Interpretation, etc., of standing orders
text: If a question arises about the application or interpretation of certified standing orders, an employer, workman, or trade union/representative body may refer it to a Labour Court under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, notified by the appropriate Government for this purpose; the Labour Court's decision, after hearing both sides, is final and binding.
plain_english_summary: Gives a clear dispute-resolution path for disagreements over what certified standing orders actually mean or how they apply, routing such questions to a designated Labour Court.

title: Act not to apply to certain industrial establishments
text: The Act does not apply to an industrial establishment insofar as its workmen are governed by specified civil-service rules — the Fundamental and Supplementary Rules, Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, Civil Services (Temporary Service) Rules, Revised Leave Rules, Civil Service Regulations, Civilians in Defence Service rules, the Indian Railway Establishment Code, or any other rules the appropriate Government notifies for this purpose.
plain_english_summary: Exempts government/civil-service workers who are already governed by their own comprehensive service rules from also being covered by this Act's standing-orders regime.

title: Power to exempt
text: The appropriate Government may, by notification, exempt (conditionally or unconditionally) any industrial establishment or class of establishments from all or any of the Act's provisions.
plain_english_summary: Gives the appropriate Government broad discretion to exempt particular establishments or categories of establishments from the Act, in whole or in part.

title: Delegation of powers
text: The appropriate Government may direct that any power it holds under the Act or its rules is also exercisable by a subordinate officer or authority — or, where the Central Government is appropriate, also by a State Government or its subordinate officer — subject to specified conditions.
plain_english_summary: Allows the appropriate Government to delegate its powers under the Act down the administrative chain, or to State Governments, for practical administration.

title: Power to make rules
text: The appropriate Government may, after previous publication, make rules by notification to carry out the Act's purposes.

sub_structure.2a_e: Such rules may in particular: prescribe additional Schedule matters and the procedure for modifying standing orders to match; set out model standing orders; prescribe Certifying Officer/appellate authority procedure; prescribe fees for register copies; and cover any other prescribable matter; representatives of employers and workmen must be consulted before rules adding Schedule matters are made.
sub_structure.3: (3) Every rule made by the Central Government must be laid before each House of Parliament for thirty days, with Parliament able to modify or annul it, without affecting anything already validly done under the rule.

plain_english_summary: Gives the appropriate Government the rule-making power needed to flesh out the Act's operational details — including expanding the Schedule and setting model standing orders — with mandatory consultation of both sides of industry and, for Central rules, parliamentary review.

title: Matters to be provided in standing orders under this Act
text: The Schedule (referenced in sections 2(g) and 3(2)) lists the topics that standing orders must cover where applicable to the establishment.

sub_structure.list: These are: classification of workmen (permanent, temporary, apprentices, probationers, or badlis); how periods/hours of work, holidays, pay-days and wage rates are communicated to workmen; shift working; attendance and late-coming; leave and holiday application procedure and granting authority; entry-gate and search requirements; closing/re-opening of sections and temporary work stoppages, with the resulting rights and liabilities of employer and workmen; termination of employment and required notice; suspension or dismissal for misconduct, and what counts as misconduct; means of redress for workmen against unfair treatment or wrongful exactions; and any other prescribed matter.

plain_english_summary: Sets out the concrete list of workplace-rule topics — from job classification and work hours to misconduct, termination, and grievance redress — that every employer's standing orders must address.

title: Short title and extent

sub_structure.1: (1) These rules may be called the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Central Rules, 1946.
sub_structure.2: (2) They extend to all Union territories, and also apply in any other State to industrial establishments under the control of the Central Government, a Railway administration, or in a major port, mine or oilfield.

plain_english_summary: Names these central rules and defines their reach: all Union territories, plus Central Government/Railway/major port/mine/oilfield establishments anywhere else in India.

title: Definitions
text: In these rules, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context:

sub_structure.a: "Act" means the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946.
sub_structure.b: "Form" means a form set out in Schedule II appended to these rules.

plain_english_summary: Defines 'Act' (the parent 1946 Act) and 'Form' (the templates in Schedule II) for purposes of these rules.

title: Additional Schedule item for coal mines
text: In the Schedule to the Act, after Item 10, an additional item (10-A) is inserted, applicable only to industrial establishments in coal mines, covering: medical aid in case of accident; railway travel facilities; method of filling vacancies; transfers; liability of the manager of the establishment or mine; service certificate; and exhibition and supply of Standing Orders.
plain_english_summary: Adds seven coal-mine-specific matters (medical aid, travel facilities, vacancy-filling, transfers, manager liability, service certificates, and standing-order display) that coal mine standing orders must additionally cover.

title: Model Standing Orders

sub_structure.1: (1) Except as otherwise provided in sub-rule (2), the Model Standing Orders for the Act's purposes are those set out in Schedule I to these rules.
sub_structure.2: (2) The Model Standing Orders for industrial establishments in coal mines are those set out in Schedule I-A to these rules.

plain_english_summary: Designates Schedule I as the general Model Standing Orders template, and Schedule I-A as the coal-mine-specific version.

title: Application for certification of standing orders
text: An application for certification of standing orders shall be made in Form I.
plain_english_summary: Requires employers seeking certification of their standing orders to use the prescribed Form I.

title: Prescribed particulars of workmen
text: The prescribed particulars of workmen for purposes of section 3(3) of the Act shall be:

sub_structure.1: (1) total number employed,
sub_structure.2: (2) number of permanent workmen,
sub_structure.3: (3) number of temporary workmen,
sub_structure.4: (4) number of badlis or substitutes,
sub_structure.5: (5) number of probationers,
sub_structure.6: (6) number of apprentices,
sub_structure.7: (7) name of the trade union(s), if any, to which the workmen belong,
sub_structure.8: (8) remarks.

plain_english_summary: Lists the workforce breakdown (permanent, temporary, casual, badli, probationer, apprentice counts, plus union affiliation) an employer must submit alongside a standing-orders certification application.

title: Certifying Officer's action on receiving an application
text: As soon as may be after receiving an application under Rule 4, the Certifying Officer shall: (a) where a trade union of the workmen exists, forward a copy of the draft standing orders to the union with a notice in Form II; or (b) where no such union exists, call a meeting of the workmen to elect three representatives, to whom a copy of the draft standing orders and a Form II notice shall be forwarded upon their election.
plain_english_summary: Directs the Certifying Officer to notify either the existing trade union or, if none exists, three elected worker representatives, once a certification application is received.

title: Authentication and forwarding of certified standing orders
text: Standing orders certified under section 5(3) or section 6(2) of the Act shall be authenticated by the signature and seal of the Certifying Officer or appellate authority, and forwarded within a week by registered post to the employer and to the trade union or elected worker representatives.
plain_english_summary: Requires certified standing orders to be officially authenticated and sent by registered post to the employer and worker representatives within a week.

title: Procedure for appeals under section 6(1) of the Act

sub_structure.1: (1) An appellant under section 6(1) of the Act must draw up a memorandum of appeal (in Form IV) setting out the grounds, and forward it in quintuplicate to the appellate authority with a certified copy of the standing orders/amendments/modifications appealed against.
sub_structure.2: (2) The appellate authority, after hearing the appellant, shall confirm the Certifying Officer's standing orders/amendments/modifications unless it considers other parties should also be heard before a final decision.
sub_structure.3: (3) If the appellate authority does not confirm them, it shall fix a hearing date and direct notice to be given: to trade unions (or elected worker representatives, or the employer) if the employer or a workman appealed; to the employer and other trade unions if a trade union appealed; or to the employer and any joined workmen if worker representatives appealed.
sub_structure.4: (4) The appellant must furnish each respondent with a copy of the memorandum of appeal.
sub_structure.5: (5) The appellate authority may call for any evidence it considers necessary.
sub_structure.6: (6) On the hearing date, the appellate authority shall take such evidence as it called for or considers relevant.

plain_english_summary: Sets out the full appeal procedure against a Certifying Officer's decision: how to file (Form IV, five copies), how the appellate authority decides whether to confirm or hold a full hearing, and who must be notified depending on who appealed.

title: Register of standing orders and copying fees
text: The register required under section 8 of the Act shall be in Form III, properly bound, and the Certifying Officer shall furnish a copy of an establishment's approved standing orders to any applicant on payment of a copying fee (seventy-five paisa for the first 200 words or less, thirty-seven paisa for each additional 100 words or part thereof, calculated on approximate word count where the order exceeds five pages).
plain_english_summary: Requires the standing-orders register to be kept in Form III, and sets a per-word copying fee scale for anyone requesting a copy of an establishment's approved standing orders.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Commencement
text: These orders shall come into force on the date specified.
plain_english_summary: States that the standing orders take effect from a specified date.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Classification of workmen

sub_structure.a: (a) Workmen are classified as: permanent, probationers, badlis, temporary, casual, and apprentices.
sub_structure.b: (b) A 'permanent workman' is one engaged on a permanent basis, including anyone who has satisfactorily completed a three-month probationary period (counting breaks for sickness, accident, leave, lock-out, legal strike, or involuntary closure).
sub_structure.c: (c) A 'probationer' is provisionally employed to fill a permanent vacancy and has not completed three months' service in that post; a permanent employee made a probationer in a new post may be reverted to the old post during probation.
sub_structure.d: (d) A 'badli' is appointed in place of a temporarily absent permanent workman or probationer.
sub_structure.e: (e) A 'temporary workman' is engaged for essentially temporary work expected to finish within a limited period.
sub_structure.f: (f) A 'casual workman' has employment of a casual nature.
sub_structure.g: (g) An 'apprentice' is a learner paid an allowance during training.

plain_english_summary: Defines the six worker categories (permanent, probationer, badli, temporary, casual, apprentice) that govern which rights and notice periods apply to a given worker.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Tickets

sub_structure.1: (1) Every workman is given a permanent ticket, unless a probationer, badli, temporary worker or apprentice.
sub_structure.2: (2) Every permanent workman gets a departmental ticket showing his number, to be shown to authorised inspectors on request.
sub_structure.3: (3) Every badli gets a badli card recording days worked, surrendered on obtaining permanent employment.
sub_structure.4: (4) Every temporary workman gets a 'temporary' ticket, surrendered on discharge.
sub_structure.5: (5) Every casual worker gets a 'casual' card recording days worked.
sub_structure.6: (6) Every apprentice gets an 'apprentice' card, surrendered on obtaining permanent employment.

plain_english_summary: Requires each worker category to carry an identifying ticket or card appropriate to their employment status, tracking days worked where relevant.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Publication of working time
text: The periods and hours of work for all classes of workers in each shift shall be exhibited in English and the principal local languages on notice-boards at or near the main entrance and the time-keeper's office.
plain_english_summary: Requires posted, bilingual/multilingual notices of shift hours near the entrance and time-keeper's office.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Publication of holidays and pay-days
text: Notices specifying the establishment's holidays and pay-days shall be posted on the notice-boards.
plain_english_summary: Requires holidays and pay-day schedules to be displayed on notice-boards.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Publication of wage rates
text: Notices specifying wage rates for all classes of workmen and work shall be displayed on the notice-boards.
plain_english_summary: Requires wage rates for every worker class and job type to be publicly posted.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Shift working
text: More than one shift may be worked at the employer's discretion, with workmen liable to transfer between shifts; discontinuing shift working requires two months' written notice (unless by agreement with affected workmen); resulting retrenchment must follow the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and restarted shift working requires notice and re-employment under that Act.
plain_english_summary: Allows multi-shift working and shift transfers at the employer's discretion, but requires two months' notice to stop a shift and Industrial Disputes Act compliance for any resulting retrenchment or re-employment.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Notice of changes in shift working
text: Notice of discontinuing or restarting shift working under Standing Order 7 must be in the prescribed form, displayed on the notice-board at the main entrance, and a copy served by registered post on the secretary of any registered trade union.
plain_english_summary: Specifies how and where shift-change notices must be posted and served, including mandatory registered-post service on a registered trade union.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Attendance and late coming
text: All workmen must be at work at the fixed and notified time; late attendance is liable to deductions under the Payment of Wages Act, 1936.
plain_english_summary: Requires punctual attendance and ties late-coming to wage deductions permitted under the Payment of Wages Act.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Leave

sub_structure.1: (1) Holidays with pay are allowed under Chapter VIII of the Factories Act, 1948, and other holidays per law, contract, custom and usage.
sub_structure.2: (2) A workman applying for leave must get an order within a week (or two days before the leave start, whichever is earlier, or same-day if leave starts within three days); refusals/postponements and reasons must be recorded in a register, with a copy available to the worker on request; extension requests are similarly decided in writing.
sub_structure.3: (3) Overstaying leave without returning within 8 days and satisfactorily explaining the delay causes loss of lien on the appointment, with the worker then placed on the badli list.

plain_english_summary: Sets the leave-application and approval process (with recorded reasons for refusal), and the consequence (loss of job lien, badli-list placement) for overstaying leave without adequate explanation.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Casual leave
text: A workman may get up to 10 days' casual leave (with or without pay) per calendar year, not exceeding 3 days at a time except for sickness, intended for unforeseen circumstances, ordinarily with prior permission from the department head or prompt written notice if not possible.
plain_english_summary: Caps casual leave at 10 days a year (max 3 consecutive days barring sickness) and requires prior or prompt notice to the department head.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Payment of wages

sub_structure.1: (1) Unclaimed wages not paid on the usual pay day shall be paid on a notified weekly unclaimed-wage pay day.
sub_structure.2: (2) Wages must be paid before the expiry of the 7th day (establishments up to 1,000 workmen) or 10th day (over 1,000) after the wage period ends.

plain_english_summary: Sets timelines for paying regular and unclaimed wages, mirroring the Payment of Wages Act's 7-day/10-day deadlines based on establishment size.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Stoppage of work

sub_structure.1: (1) The employer may stop any section of the establishment without notice for reasons like fire, breakdown, power stoppage, epidemic, or civil commotion beyond their control.
sub_structure.2: (2) Affected workmen must be notified by notice-board; detention beyond 1 hour after stoppage entitles workmen to wages for the whole detention period (piece-rate workers use their average daily earning); detention under 1 hour is unpaid; no other compensation is due; short lay-offs are treated as compulsory leave (paid or unpaid); indefinite lay-offs may lead to termination with due notice or pay in lieu.
sub_structure.3: (3) Lay-off periods due to plant failure or curtailed production are treated as compulsory leave; indefinitely long lay-offs may end in termination with notice or pay.
sub_structure.4: (4) During a strike affecting a section, the employer may close that and related sections, with notice given to affected workmen before resumption.

plain_english_summary: Lets employers halt work without notice for events beyond their control, sets pay rules for workers detained during stoppages (paid after 1 hour, unpaid before), and covers lay-off and strike-related closure procedures.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Termination of employment

sub_structure.1: (1) Terminating a permanent workman requires one month's notice (monthly-rated) or two weeks' notice (others), or pay in lieu.
sub_structure.2: (2) Temporary workmen, probationers and badlis get no notice or pay in lieu on termination, but a temporary workman's services cannot be terminated as punishment without a misconduct hearing under Standing Order 14.
sub_structure.3: (3) On termination, earned wages and other dues must be paid before the expiry of the second working day after termination.

plain_english_summary: Sets notice requirements for terminating permanent workmen (1 month or 2 weeks depending on pay basis), exempts temporary/probationary/badli workers from notice (except for punitive termination), and requires final dues within two working days.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Disciplinary action for misconduct

sub_structure.1: (1) A workman may be fined up to 2% of a month's wages for specified acts/omissions notified with government approval under section 8 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936.
sub_structure.2: (2) A workman may be suspended up to 4 days at a time, or dismissed without notice or compensation, for proven misconduct.
sub_structure.3: (3) Misconduct includes: wilful insubordination or disobedience; theft, fraud or dishonesty; wilful damage to employer property; bribery; habitual unauthorised absence (or over 10 days); habitual late attendance; habitual breach of applicable law; riotous/disorderly behaviour or acts subversive of discipline; habitual negligence; repeated finable acts; and illegal strike action or incitement.
sub_structure.4a: (4)(a) A workman facing contemplated/pending disciplinary or criminal proceedings may be suspended in writing, with detailed reasons supplied within a week.
sub_structure.4b: (4)(b) Subsistence allowance during suspension: for departmental enquiries, half wages for the first 90 days, three-quarters beyond that (reduced to one-quarter if the delay is the workman's fault); for outside-agency enquiries or criminal proceedings, half wages for the first 180 days, three-quarters beyond that (similarly reduced if delay is the workman's fault).
sub_structure.4ba: (b-a) The workman may appear in person or be represented by a trade-union office-bearer during the enquiry.
sub_structure.4bb: (b-b) Enquiry proceedings shall be recorded in Hindi, English, or the local State language, per the workman's preference.
sub_structure.4bc: (b-c) The enquiry must be completed within three months, extendable for recorded reasons.
sub_structure.4c: (c) If found guilty after a hearing on the proposed penalty, the employer may order dismissal, suspension, fine, stoppage of increment, or reduction in rank, with specific back-pay/suspension-period rules depending on the outcome and any Article 311(2) Constitutional protections that apply.
sub_structure.4d: (d) If found not guilty, the workman is deemed on duty throughout the suspension and entitled to full wages minus the subsistence allowance already paid.
sub_structure.4e: (e) Subsistence allowance payment is conditional on the workman not taking other employment during suspension.
sub_structure.5: (5) Punishment decisions must consider the misconduct's gravity, the workman's prior record, and any extenuating or aggravating circumstances; a copy of the punishment order must be given to the workman.
sub_structure.6a: (6)(a) A workman aggrieved by a punishment order may appeal to the appellate authority within 21 days of receiving the order.
sub_structure.6b: (6)(b) The employer must specify who the appellate authority is.
sub_structure.6c: (6)(c) The appellate authority must hear the workman and decide the appeal within 15 days, communicating the decision in writing.

plain_english_summary: Provides the full misconduct and disciplinary framework: what counts as misconduct, fine/suspension/dismissal powers, detailed subsistence-allowance rules during suspension pending inquiry, enquiry procedure and timelines, back-pay rules depending on outcome, and a 21-day appeal right.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Complaints
text: All employment-related complaints, including unfair treatment or wrongful exaction, shall be submitted to the manager or specified person, with a right of appeal to the employer.
plain_english_summary: Gives workers a complaint channel to the manager with a further appeal right to the employer.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Certificate on termination of service
text: Every permanent workman is entitled to a service certificate on dismissal, discharge or retirement.
plain_english_summary: Guarantees a permanent workman a service certificate whenever their employment ends.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Liability of employer
text: The employer of the establishment is personally responsible for the proper and faithful observance of the standing orders.
plain_english_summary: Makes the employer personally accountable for ensuring the standing orders are actually followed.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Appeal procedure (duplicate of Rule 7-A)
text: Sets out the same appeal procedure as Rule 7-A: memorandum of appeal in quintuplicate with certified copy of the standing orders, hearing by the appellate authority, notice to affected parties, and evidence-taking at the hearing.
plain_english_summary: Restates the standing-orders appeal procedure (memorandum of appeal, hearing, notice to parties) within the Model Standing Orders themselves.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS NOT BEING INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Exhibition of standing orders
text: A copy of these orders in English and Hindi shall be posted on a notice-board at or near the main entrance and kept legible.
plain_english_summary: Requires the standing orders themselves to be permanently and legibly displayed in English and Hindi at the establishment's entrance.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Commencement
text: These orders shall come into force on the date specified.
plain_english_summary: States that the coal-mine standing orders take effect from a specified date.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Definitions

sub_structure.a: (a) 'attendance' means presence at the required place for work with attendance marked.
sub_structure.b: (b) 'employer' and 'workman' carry the meanings in sections 2(d) and 2(i) of the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946.
sub_structure.c: (c) 'Manager' means the mine's manager, including an acting manager appointed under the Mines Act, 1952.
sub_structure.e: (e) Singular includes plural and vice versa.

plain_english_summary: Defines attendance, employer/workman (by cross-reference to the parent Act), manager, and standard gender/number interpretation rules for the coal mine standing orders.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Classification of workmen

sub_structure.a: (a) Workmen are classified as: permanent, probationers, badlis/substitutes, temporary, apprentices, and casual.
sub_structure.b: (b) A 'permanent workman' is appointed for an unlimited period or has completed 3 months' continuous service as a probationer in a permanent post.
sub_structure.c: (c) A 'probationer' provisionally fills a permanent vacancy and has under 3 months' service in that post (extendable); a permanent workman made probationer in a new post may revert during probation.
sub_structure.d: (d) A 'badli/substitute' fills in for a temporarily absent permanent workman/probationer, ceasing to be a badli after one year's continuous service (190 attendances below ground, 240 otherwise) in the same/similar post, or becoming permanent after completing a probationer's term.
sub_structure.e: (e) A 'temporary' workman is engaged for essentially temporary work with a specified (extendable) likely finish period.
sub_structure.f: (f) An 'apprentice' is a learner, paid or unpaid, per their training contract terms.
sub_structure.g: (g) A 'casual' workman is engaged for essentially casual work.

plain_english_summary: Defines six coal-mine worker categories, with badli status converting to permanent after specified continuous service thresholds (190/240 attendances or one year).

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Tickets
text: Every workman is given a classification-appropriate ticket at appointment, bearing their signature/thumb-impression, shown to authorised persons on request; a lost ticket is replaced for 25 paisa.
plain_english_summary: Requires signed/thumb-printed identity tickets for every coal-mine worker, replaceable for a small fee if lost.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Display of notices
text: Shift periods/hours, holidays, pay-days, and wage rates/allowance scales shall be displayed in English and the majority local language on notice-boards at the main entrance and time-keeper's office.
plain_english_summary: Requires bilingual posting of shift hours, holidays, pay-days, and wage rates at the mine entrance and time-keeper's office.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Payment of wages

sub_structure.a: (a) Wages are paid directly to workmen on a working day between 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. at the mine office, witnessed and attested by the manager or an authorised person; contractor's workmen are paid at a manager-specified place, witnessed by an employer's nominee.
sub_structure.b: (b) Unclaimed wages are paid on a notified weekly unclaimed-wage day, or remitted by money order (minus commission) on request, with claims presentable within 12 months of falling due.
sub_structure.c: (c) Overtime is worked and paid per the Mines Act, 1952 (as amended); weekly-rest-day work is paid per agreement, award, usage or custom.

plain_english_summary: Sets wage payment timing, witnessing/attestation requirements, unclaimed-wage handling, and overtime pay rules tied to the Mines Act.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Shift working
text: Mirrors the general Schedule I shift-working rule: multiple shifts allowed at employer discretion with worker transfer liability; two months' notice needed to discontinue a shift (unless by agreement); retrenchment/re-employment from shift changes follows the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
plain_english_summary: Applies the same multi-shift and two-month-notice framework as the general standing orders, tied to Industrial Disputes Act compliance for related retrenchment.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Attendance
text: All workmen must be at work at the mine at the fixed, notified time.
plain_english_summary: Requires punctual attendance at the mine.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Absence from place of work
text: A workman found absent from their proper work post during working hours without permission or sufficient reason is treated as absent for that period.
plain_english_summary: Treats unauthorised absence from one's post (even while technically at the mine) as absence for pay purposes.

chapter_title: MODEL STANDING ORDERS FOR INDUSTRIAL ESTABLISHMENTS IN COAL MINES
title: Festival holidays and leave

sub_structure.a: (a) Seven paid festival holidays apply (Republic Day, Independence Day, and Gandhi's Birthday mandatory; the rest by agreement/local custom); working on a holiday earns triple pay, or double pay plus a substituted paid holiday.
sub_structure.b1: (b)(i) Leave with wages follows Chapter VII of the Mines Act, 1952.
sub_structure.b2: (b)(ii) Leave applied for is normally granted, though the employer may refuse/revoke/curtail it for work exigencies, with wages in lieu paid where refused or unaccumulable, and a railway-concession makeup mechanism if leave is refused one year.
sub_structure.c: (c) Quarantine leave is granted (on a medical certificate) for contagious-disease exposure through no fault of the worker, paid at 50% of wages, unless the worker previously refused prophylactic treatment.
sub_structure.d: (d) Leave applications must be made at least 15 days ahead (except unforeseen circumstances), decided within a week (or by two days before leave start, whichever is earlier, or same-day if leave starts within 3 days), with refusals/postponements and reasons recorded in writing.
sub_structure.e: (e) Overstaying leave beyond 10 days without satisfactory explanation causes loss of job lien, placing the worker on the badli list.
sub_structure.f: (f) Casual leave with pay is capped at 5 days a year, max 3 consecutive days except for sickness, requiring prior (or prompt written) notice.
